Over the last 800,000 years, Earth’s climate has experienced periodic glacial and interglacial cycles driven by orbital parameters, CO 2 concentrations, and ice sheet volumes.
These climate simulation datasets include global annual mean surface temperature and precipitation distributions with a horizontal resolution of 3.75°.

Overall, these simulations provide a reliable and verifiable climate dataset, offering strong support for studying the driving mechanisms of past glacial-interglacial climate changes and interpreting long-term climate signals in geological records.

In recent decades, with the continuous emergence of a large number of high-resolution geological evidence, including marine sediments, ice cores, loess deposits, and speleothems, these records carry key information about atmospheric and oceanic circulation at high and low latitudes, greatly deepening our understanding of global climate changes on the orbital scale since the Pleistocene.

Recent findings suggest spatial decoupling: the glacial cycles (~100-kyr) modulate precipitation via land-sea thermal gradients, whereas precession (~20-kyr) drives Intertropical Convergence Zone migrations and frontal rainfall intensity 13 .

Furthermore, a series of high-resolution records have revealed the long-term characteristics of changes in the Southern and Northern Hemisphere westerlies 15 , widespread Asian arid events 14 , tropical Pacific Walker circulation 16 , Hadley circulation 17 , Intertropical Convergence Zone 18 , and Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) 19 .

However, the spatial distribution limitations of continental and oceanic records have, to some extent, restricted our in-depth understanding of the evolutionary characteristics and dynamics of orbital-scale climate change over the past 800,000 years of the Pleistocene.

784ka Equilibrium Experiment Setup The initiation time for the past 800,000-year transient experiments was chosen with the following considerations: (1) The equilibrium slice experiment, serving as the foundation for transient simulations, required sufficient integration duration to achieve a quasi-equilibrium state.

Since this slice experiment was initialized with modern boundary conditions, selecting the first interglacial period (~800 ka) rather than a glacial period as the starting point avoids substantial adjustments to boundary conditions (e.g., orbital parameters, global ice volume, and CO₂ concentration), thereby accelerating equilibration; (2) Following the simulation start time of previous studies 70 , the equilibrium climate of 784,000 years ago was chosen as the initial state for the transient experiments.

It is evident that our transient simulation based on a complex climate model has successfully reproduced the rapid cooling signals in high latitudes during glacial-interglacial cycles.
We caution that the simulated AMOC responses to climatic forcing may not fully capture the transient feedback mechanisms operating within the actual climate system.

Comparative analysis of individual and full forcing experiments demonstrates that the 100-kyr periodicity of the North Atlantic high-latitude SST variability is predominantly regulated by ice sheet dynamics (Figure S13a ), which modulate ocean circulation and SSTs via topographic effects and albedo feedbacks; while orbital forcing (Figure S13c ) plays a secondary role in modulating these signals, while CO₂ forcing (Figure S13b ) demonstrates negligible contributions.
